doc.title: Stanley Dance interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

chapter: Growing up with jazz in England
title: Boarding-school records, discovering jazz, and Ellington's 1933 London visit
summary: Dance heard jazz on radio and via schoolmates who brought home records by Morton, Red Nichols and others; interest grew via Melody Maker. He recalls Ellington's 1933 Trocadero concerts and arguing with Fats Waller about growling on alto.

bands.name: Jelly Roll Morton and his Red Hot Peppers

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Well radio of course. You’d hear jazz of the time on the radio. Then by a lucky chance, my father sent me away to a boarding school, where the sons of several of the directors of the leading record companies were also sent. Now these kids came back each term with all the records. Most kids brought back the records they liked, which was the pop records, and you’d be sick of them you know after two or three times. But these kids would have weird records by Jelly Roll Morton and his Hot Peppers. We were very fond of another one called Bobby Lechens Leidmore Band, which was a washboard band. We had Red Nichols and his Five Pennies and so forth and so on. These records were, at the beginning of the term were not played because people put them on and would say, “I don’t like that.” But after three or four weeks of the pop hits you were sick of them. And then various people would put these strange records on. And the school was divided into four houses. And each house had a room for entertainment. And in each of them as I remember there would be some boys that would be attracted to this music. Sometimes for rather strange reasons. I remember that Benny Moten’s band in Kansas City made a record called “Thick Lip Stomp.” And there was one boy that had thick lips. He wasn’t black or Negro as we said at that time at all, but he was known as Thick Lip Liggert. And when they found this record, “Thick Lip Stomp,” every time he came in the room somebody would make a dash to play this record just to irritate the hell out of him. But

from this grew a sort of more intelligent interest in music. There was, early on in England there was the paper called The Melody Maker which had record reviews which were fairly hip. But the influence in England to begin with was mainly coming from, well very often came from New York musicians who were playing in The Savoy Hotel and places like that. They came over and they were full of we’ll say Red Nichols, Joe Venuti, Ed Lang and people like that. But the black musicians were considered, for a long time, somewhat crude. And it wasn’t until I guess almost 1930 that we began to discover this music with a little more serious intent. And then — there was nevertheless quite a big interest in jazz in England, as in France. And then the musicians started to come over — Louis Armstrong came, Fats Waller came, and then in 1933 Duke Ellington came. And that later became my main thing. That was unquestionably the biggest sensation any jazz group ever made in England. They played at The Palladium, which was a sort of vaudeville house. And they would play a set of about 40 minutes or so. And that was not enough for the audience. The musicians knew of Ellington by then, and there was a big clamor for better presentation. And The Melody Maker organized two concerts in The Trocadero, which was the biggest movie house in Europe. And it was packed and jammed. And the first concert was sold out, and Duke knew they wanted to hear what they called the real thing you know. They didn’t want to hear “Stormy Weather” again. They wanted to hear his compositions. They played an excellent program. At the second concert he couldn’t really believe it. He’d compromised a bit. He played some of the more popular things. But that was a sensation. They looked very smart, they were well dressed in sort of light colored, fawn colored suits as I remember, with orange ties — and you know we just thought that looked very, very — in fact, many of his fans wore orange ties for quite a long time after that. Well I really only said hello to Duke on that occasion. But then I remember meeting, somehow or other, Fats Waller when he was there, and that was very instructive. I went back stage where he was playing and got into an argument with somebody. It must have been around ‘37 or ‘36 I guess. Oh there was another famous writer there called Ian Mag, he was backstage too, and that was — there was a record had come out with Benny Carter playing alto on this record called “Apologies.” And he started out with a sort of growl on the alto you know. And I said something about this growl. And Ian says, “You growl on a trumpet, Stanley, or a trombone, not on a saxophone.” And Fats said, “You can growl on any instrument if you know how.” It was a splendid, just — so well I’m buying records all this time, and my friends and I decided we couldn’t get — they weren’t issuing enough. We started to import them from I remember for some reason, a record store called Royer Smith in Philadelphia, who sent us the catalogues.
